questions.q: What most distinguishes an agent from a workflow?
options: An agent uses a language model, while a workflow never includes an AI step
An agent runs on a schedule, while a workflow only runs when a form is submitted
In an agent, the model decides the steps at run time; in a workflow, you decide them in advance
An agent is always cheaper and faster than a workflow because it skips unneeded steps
questions.explain: The lesson defines the difference by who chooses the steps: you design a workflow's steps in advance, while an agent's model chooses them as it goes, trading predictability for flexibility.

questions.q: You want to route every new form submission to one of three sales reps by region, and you could draw the flowchart in five minutes. What does the four-question test suggest?
options: Build it as a workflow, because a task you can map in advance doesn't need an agent
Build an agent with broad tools so it can handle any future routing rule
Build an agent but cap it at ten steps so its costs stay predictable
Skip automation entirely, because routing decisions always need a person
questions.explain: The first question asks whether the task is genuinely multi-step and hard to spell out in advance; if you can draw the flowchart, the lesson says to build the workflow.

questions.q: Which of these tasks is the best fit for an agent, according to the lesson?
options: Sending the same welcome email to every new subscriber the moment they sign up
Replying to website chats within a second, with identical compliance wording each time
Tagging a handful of invoices a month that a person can sort quickly by hand
Working out why an invoice doesn't match its order by checking two or three systems
questions.explain: Agents shine on tasks with variable paths that require looking things up, like operations investigations, while fixed sequences, strict compliance, split-second responses and very low volumes are red flags.
